content: PAK1, a serine/threonine-protein kinase, is an enzyme encoded by the PAK1 gene in humans. It belongs to the PAK family of serine/threonine kinases, which consists of six members divided into two groups: Group I (PAK1, PAK2, and PAK3) and Group II (PAK4, PAK5/7, and PAK6). These kinases are evolutionarily conserved. PAK1 is localized in distinct subcellular domains within the cytoplasm and nucleus. It plays a critical role in regulating cytoskeletal remodeling, phenotypic signaling, and gene expression, influencing various cellular processes such as directional motility, invasion, metastasis, growth, cell cycle progression, and angiogenesis. PAK1-dependent signaling is involved in both physiological and pathological processes, including cancer, where PAK1 is frequently overexpressed and hyperactivated. PAK1 was first identified in 1994 by Manser and colleagues as an effector of Rho GTPases in rat brain. The human PAK1 was later discovered in 1995 by Martin and colleagues as a GTP-dependent interacting partner of Rac1 or Cdc42 in neutrophils, with its complementary DNA cloned from a human placenta library. PAK proteins, including PAK1, PAK2, PAK3, and PAK4, are critical effectors linking the Rho family of GTPases to cytoskeletal reorganization and nuclear signaling. These proteins serve as targets for small GTP-binding proteins such as Cdc42 and Rac and are implicated in a wide range of biological activities. PAK1 specifically regulates cell motility and morphology. Alternative transcripts of the PAK1 gene have been identified, but their full-length structures remain undetermined. Activation of PAK1 is associated with fundamental cellular processes essential for life. As a nodal signaling molecule, PAK1 integrates signals from cell surface proteins and upstream activators, translating them into specific phenotypic outcomes. Biochemically, PAK1 exerts its effects by phosphorylating effector substrates, initiating cascades of biochemical events that culminate in cellular phenotypic responses. Additionally, PAK1's scaffolding activity also influences its function. PAK1-regulated cellular processes include actin and microtubule dynamics, cell cycle progression, motility, invasion, redox and energy metabolism, cell survival, angiogenesis, DNA repair, hormone sensitivity, and gene expression. PAK1 signaling has functional implications in oncogenesis, viral pathogenesis, cardiovascular dysregulation, and neurological disorders. The human PAK1 gene spans 153 kilobases and contains 23 exons, with six exons for the 5’-UTR and 17 exons for protein coding. Of the 20 spliced transcripts identified, only 12 have open reading frames, coding for 10 proteins and two polypeptides. The remaining eight transcripts are non-coding long RNAs, ranging from 308 to 863 base pairs in length. The core domains of PAK family proteins include a kinase domain in the C-terminal region, a p21-binding domain (PBD), and an auto-inhibitory domain (AID) in Group I PAKs. Group I PAKs exist in an inactive, closed homodimer conformation, where the AID of one molecule binds to the kinase domain of another. Activation occurs through both GTPase-dependent and -independent mechanisms. PAK1 contains an auto-inhibitory domain that suppresses the catalytic activity of its kinase domain. Activators of PAK1 relieve this auto-inhibition, triggering conformational rearrangements and autophosphorylation events that lead to kinase activation. IPA-3 is a known inhibitor of PAK1, but preactivated PAK1 is resistant to IPA-3. Inhibition of PAK1 in live cells highlights its critical role in PDGF-stimulated ERK activation. IPA-3 binds reversibly to the PAK1 regulatory domain, preventing GTPase docking and subsequent activation. PAK1 knockdown in prostate cancer cells reduces motility, decreases MMP9 secretion, and increases TGFβ expression, which is growth inhibitory in these contexts. However, IPA-3's pharmacokinetic limitations and undesirable redox effects make it unsuitable for clinical development. PAK1 activity is stimulated by numerous upstream activators and signals, including EGF, heregulin-beta 1, VEGF, basic fibroblast growth factor, platelet-derived growth factor, estrogen, lysophosphatidic acid, phosphoinositides, ETK, AKT, JAK2, ERK, casein kinase II, Rac3, chemokine (C-X-C motif) ligand 1, breast cancer anti-estrogen resistance 3, Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus-G protein-coupled receptor, ARG-binding protein 2γ, hepatitis B virus X protein, STE20-related kinase adaptor protein α, RhoI, Klotho, N-acetylglucosaminyl transferase V, B-Raf proto-oncogene, casein kinase 2-interacting protein 1, and filamin A. PAK1 functions are regulated by its ability to phosphorylate downstream effector substrates, scaffold activity, redistribution to distinct subcellular domains, and modulation of genomic target expression. Representative PAK1 effector substrates in cancer cells include Stathmin-S16, Merlin-S518, Vimentin-S25/S38/S50/S65/S72, Histone H3-S10, Filamin A-S2152, Estrogen receptor-alpha-S305, Signal transducer and activator of transcription 5a-S779, C-terminal binding protein 1-S158, Raf1-S338, Arpc1b-T21, DLC1-S88, Phosphoglucomutase 1-T466, SMART/HDAC1-associated repressor protein-S3486/T3568, Tubulin Cofactor B-S65/S128, Snail-S246, Vascular endothelial-cadherin-S665, Poly(RC) binding protein 1-T60/S246, Integrin-linked kinase 1-T173/S246, Epithelium-specific Ets transcription factor 1-S207, ErbB3 binding protein 1-T261, Nuclear receptor-interacting factor 3-S28, SRC3-delta4-T56/S659/S676, Beta-catenin-S675, BAD-S111/S112/S136, MEK1-S298, CRKII-S41, MORC family CW-type zinc finger 2-S739, Paxillin-S258/S273. PAK1 and its dependent signals modulate the expression of genomic targets, including vascular endothelial growth factor, Cyclin D1, phosphofructokinase-muscle isoform, nuclear factor of activated T-cell, Cyclin B1, Tissue Factor, Tissue Factor Pathway Inhibitor, Metalloproteinase 9, and fibronectin. PAK1 has been shown to interact with ARHGEF2, ARPC1B, BMX, C-Raf, CDC42, Cyclin-dependent kinase 5, DYNL1, LIMK1, NCK1, PAK1IP1, and RAC1.
